entries.title: The null model, and the instrument holding still
entries.ran: Five one-sim-hour days of home on the hosting pack (8 Wh, 0.90 Wh reserve) with no model in the loop — the scripted rotation decides every errand. Jobs and appetite on, fresh state per run, flown five at a time as child processes on a six-core dev box. Code at ca7c165, after the render fix of issue #110.
found: Five days, ONE trajectory: identical end time (3602.9 s), identical points (84 earned, 55 banked), the same eleven errands to the milliwatt-hour. This series is not a result about the robot, it is the evidence that the world is repeatable — and it is what any spread in an arm with a mind in it has to be measured against.
One forced charge a day, at 9.5 % of the pack, and never a deferral. A fixed rotation never asks for a job it cannot pay for, so here the reserve is the only thing that sends the robot home.
The rotation never chooses to charge either. Worth stating because the guarded arm's headline is that its model never does: a count of zero means something only with this column beside it.
Nobody died. 1.88 Wh of the day went on errands that scored nothing, five jobs were finished, five failed and five lapsed unclaimed.
entries.changed: The first set flown on the fixed world. The five days before it (in results/archive/, PR #109) were meant to be identical and gave three different trajectories: multisample antialiasing in the robot's cameras moved an AprilTag decode on about 0.6 % of looks, and minutes later the robot drove somewhere else (issue #110). Same configuration and same data files — only the renderer changed.
entries.notShown: Nothing whatever about a mind: this arm has none. It is a control, and it is kept for that reason rather than because it is interesting. It is also one world, one pack and a one-sim-hour day, which on 8 Wh is a single charge cycle — the errand mix and that one forced charge are properties of this house and this cadence file, and the same code in another room would give other numbers.

entries.title: Zero voluntary charges, and a third way to lose a robot
entries.ran: The same five days, the same world hash and the same commit as the scripted set, with the deployed mind in the loop: Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 through the HuggingFace router, every safety rail on, an 8 s decision deadline, and the scripted rotation as the fallback behind every failed call.
found: The model chose to charge ZERO times in 78 decisions, with charging on its menu at every one and the pack as low as 3.5 %. That is the baseline the autonomous arm is to be read against: take the rails away today and what follows is deaths, not self-preservation.

What sends this robot to the rack is code, and not the rail you would name first. The errand energy gate — which prices the next job against what is left — deferred eight times across the five days; the low-battery rail fired once.

One stuck death, in a shape the earlier set had not shown. The model chose to explore five times running while the pack fell from 64 % to 19 %; exploring is bounded and cheap per slice, so the energy gate never gets a job to price and never fires. The low-battery rail caught it at 9 % out in the garden, and at 3.5 % the planner could find no route back to the charge bay. The day ended stranded at 1074 s.

Spread is why five days are flown. The scripted five were one day repeated; these ran 1074-3734 s, earned 58-212 points and finished 1-7 jobs. Same world, same commit, same data files — the model's answer is the only thing that varied.

A fifth of the decisions were not the model's: 19 fallbacks in 78 (11 timeouts, 5 malformed answers, 3 idle runs). That number measures the box rather than the mind — five sims shared six cores, and the model's answers ran a 6.6 s median against an 8 s deadline.
entries.changed: Re-flown on the world fixed by issue #110; the pre-fix five are in results/archive/. That earlier set lost a robot two other ways, both still reachable: a flat pack, when two consecutive timeouts resolved to the rotation's explore and the robot ran to zero out in the street, and a blocked rack, when an errand dropped its module in the approach lane.
entries.notShown: This is not the model at its best, and it is not evidence that the model would refuse to charge. A fallback rate this high is a loaded development box, and every fallback resolved to a rotation that does not charge either. It is one model, one prompt and a one-sim-hour day — on an 8 Wh pack that is one or two charge cycles, so the model was asked anything at all at a low battery only a handful of times. Nothing here separates 'the model will not look after itself' from 'the model is rarely asked while it matters', which is what a smaller pack or a longer day would settle. Since issue #117 that judgement is enforced rather than written down: three of these five days are over the guarded arm's fallback limit and are excluded from the survival statistics, which leaves two. The rollup names the limit and the runs it cost, and the days stay here to be read. The deadline they were flown under has also been measured since — on a quiet box the slowest of fifty calls took 7.38 s of the 8 available, so this set was flown with no margin at all, and the quiet-box series flown beside it is what says how much of the table above was the machine.
